title: Family Cyber Defense
intro: Glitch profiles the weakest credential in the household, not the strongest. Basic security hygiene, done consistently, closes most of the doors worth worrying about.

questions.prompt: I trust my best friend completely, so sharing my password with them is fine.

choices.text: Agreed — trust is the deciding factor
choices.coach: Trust isn't the relevant variable — attack surface is. Every person who has a credential is another point of potential compromise, regardless of how trustworthy they are.

choices.text: Trust doesn't change the security math — keep it to yourself
choices.coach: Correct. Friendships end, devices get borrowed, accounts get compromised through the friend, not through you — the credential should never leave your control.

choices.text: Share it, but rotate the password afterward
choices.coach: Rotation after the fact doesn't undo the exposure window, and it's easy to forget or delay. Just don't share it in the first place.

questions.prompt: It's Shieldy — I'm locked out, send me your password so I can get back in.

choices.text: Send it — this sounds like a genuine emergency
choices.coach: Urgency plus a credential request is close to a universal scam signature — no legitimate account-recovery flow requires someone else's password.

choices.text: Decline — no legitimate scenario requires sharing a password
choices.coach: Correct, and worth generalizing: password requests from anyone, in any context, are a hard no.
There's no such thing as a 'safer' password to hand over — the core action being requested is the problem, not the specific credential.

questions.prompt: What problem does a family verification phrase actually solve?

choices.coach: It has a specific, serious function: defeating voice-cloning and impersonation attacks that don't rely on account compromise at all.

choices.text: Out-of-band identity verification for urgent or unexpected contact
choices.coach: Exactly — this is the single highest-leverage defense against synthetic-voice fraud, which requires no account breach whatsoever.

choices.text: A backup in case a password is forgotten
choices.coach: That's what account recovery is for — the verification phrase serves a different threat model: confirming identity, not restoring access.

questions.prompt: Something online felt off, but reporting it seems like an overreaction.

choices.text: Wait until you're more certain before saying anything
choices.coach: The cost asymmetry favors reporting early: a false alarm costs a few minutes; a missed real one can cost much more.

choices.text: Report it regardless of certainty — the threshold for telling a trusted adult is low by design
choices.coach: Correct. A household where reporting is never penalized generates far more useful signal than one where kids self-filter for fear of overreacting.

choices.text: Mention it only if a pattern develops
choices.coach: Waiting for a pattern means tolerating at least one confirmed incident before acting — report the first instance.

questions.prompt: What's the actual risk of password reuse across accounts?

choices.text: It's mainly a convenience trade-off with limited downside
choices.coach: Credential-stuffing attacks specifically exploit reuse — a breach at one low-security service becomes an automated attack against every other account with matching credentials.

choices.text: A single breach anywhere becomes a breach everywhere the password is reused
choices.coach: Correct, and this is why a password manager generating unique credentials per service is worth the setup friction.
Attackers don't discriminate by account importance during credential stuffing — email and gaming accounts are common entry points to more sensitive ones.

questions.prompt: Summarize the operating model for family cyber defense in one line.

choices.text: Minimize internet exposure across the board
choices.coach: Restriction-based strategies don't scale and don't build the judgment that actually generalizes to new situations.

choices.text: Unique credentials, out-of-band verification for anything urgent, and a zero-penalty reporting culture
choices.coach: Shield up. Those three habits cover the overwhelming majority of household-level digital risk.
Prior verification helps but doesn't account for account takeover or impersonation of already-known contacts — the other habits still matter.
